key_insight: AI-translated literary texts can be acceptable on standard translation criteria, but readers still tend to prefer human translations for immersion and literary feel. The paper shows that “fine” machine output does not necessarily equal a satisfying reading experience.
problem_solved: This paper addresses the gap between conventional translation evaluation and how people actually experience literary translations. It asks whether AI translations preserve not just meaning and fluency, but also the immersive, aesthetic qualities that matter in literature.
method: Recruit 15 avid readers to compare recently published human translations with machine translations.
Use machine translations produced by an agentic LLM-based pipeline.
Collect reader judgments focused on immersion, literary effect, and overall preference rather than only adequacy/fluency metrics.
impact: For AI/ML practitioners, this highlights that benchmark scores can miss what users value in creative language tasks. It suggests that evaluation of literary translation should include human-centered, experience-based measures, not just automatic metrics.

paper_title: AI translation of literary texts is "fine", but readers still prefer human translations
